name: Aglaophyton
fact: One of the first complex plants to colonize dry land, with branching stems but no true leaves or roots. Its fossils from Scotland preserve the world's oldest known mycorrhizal fungi inside its cells - proving that the plant-fungi partnership is as ancient as plant life on land itself.

name: Dunkleosteus
size: About 3.5–4 m (older books: up to 9 m)
fact: An armoured fish with no teeth: its jaws carried bony blades that sharpened against each other as it bit, and its bite was one of the most powerful of any fish. A top predator of the Late Devonian seas.
know: It had no teeth: the “fangs” are self-sharpening blades of jaw bone. Only its armoured head fossilises, so its length is an estimate — and a 2023 restudy cut it from the 9 m of older books to about 3.5–4 m: shorter, but built like a giant tuna.

name: Tiktaalik
c: Fishes › Lobe-finned fishes › Fish with limbs
fact: Fin structures show true digits — proto-hands and feet. It could breathe air and navigate shallow river channels.
know: It was predicted before it was found. Neil Shubin's team reasoned that a fish-to-land animal should lie in river rocks about 375 million years old, found such rocks exposed in Arctic Canada, and searched for four summers. The name is Inuktitut for a large freshwater fish.
discovery: Three fossils found 2004 in Fram Formation, Ellesmere Island, Canada. Described 2006 in Nature.
keyResearchers: Daeschler, E.B., Shubin, N.H., & Jenkins Jr., F.A. (2006)
citation: Daeschler et al. (2006). A Devonian tetrapod-like fish. Nature 440:757–763.

name: Stethacanthus
fact: An early shark with a bizarre flat-topped anvil-shaped structure on its back. We still don't know exactly what it was for — maybe display? Maybe defense? Even today sharks are amazing survivors, little changed in 400 million years.

name: Archaeopteris Tree
fact: The first real forests! These trees were so new that no microbes had evolved to decompose wood yet. When a tree fell, it just lay there for millions of years. Most of the coal we burn today is made from these very forests!

name: Eusthenopteron
fact: A lobe-finned fish with primitive limbs in its fins! It could breathe air and walked on land. On the direct evolutionary path to tetrapods (four-legged animals). The bridge between fish and land creatures.

name: Lungfish (Dipnoi)
fact: The only group of lobe-finned fish to survive to today! They have both gills AND lungs. During dry seasons, they burrow into mud and breathe air in a cocoon. Living relics of the fish-to-land transition.

name: Cladoselache
fact: One of the earliest true sharks with a streamlined body and forked tail almost identical to a modern mako shark. Fossils preserve soft tissue including kidney-shaped muscles along the body, showing sharks had already found their near-perfect body plan 375 million years ago.

name: Bothriolepis
fact: A box-shaped armored placoderm with jointed pectoral fins that functioned almost like arms, letting it prop itself up on the river bottom. Bothriolepis may also have had primitive lungs, giving it the ability to gulp air and survive in stagnant oxygen-poor water.

name: Acanthostega
c: Amphibians & early tetrapods › First four-legged animals
fact: A transitional tetrapod with four fully formed limbs but also gills - meaning it could NOT survive on land despite having legs! Its eight-fingered hands were used for gripping underwater plants rather than walking. Acanthostega proves that limbs evolved for aquatic life long before any creature walked on land.

name: Pteraspis
fact: A streamlined jawless fish with a bullet-shaped head shield that reduced drag as it swam. Thousands of its fossils are found together in mass-death layers, suggesting it schooled in enormous groups like modern herring.

name: Prototaxites
fact: The tallest living thing on land in its day: a trunk-like pillar with no leaves or branches, made of tangled tubes.
debate: Long called a giant fungus. A study published in 2026 found its structure and chemistry did not match fungi either — it may belong to a lineage of life with no living members.

name: Wattieza
fact: The oldest known tree: a palm-like trunk with fronds on top. Stumps found at Gilboa, New York, in the 1870s were finally matched to their crowns in 2007.

name: Rhyniognatha
fact: A pair of tiny jaws in the Rhynie Chert — possibly the oldest insect known.
debate: Insect, or a centipede-like relative? A 2017 restudy argued for the latter; the question is open.

name: Coccosteus
fact: A small cousin of Dunkleosteus with self-sharpening jaw plates and a joint that let its head tip back to open its mouth extra wide.

name: Titanichthys
fact: A giant armoured fish with weak, toothless jaws: a plankton-eater, like a basking shark, sharing the sea with Dunkleosteus.

name: Materpiscis
fact: Its name means “mother fish”: the fossil holds an embryo still attached by a mineralised umbilical cord — the oldest known live birth.

name: Panderichthys
c: Fishes › Lobe-finned fishes › Fish with limbs
fact: A flat-headed fish with eyes on top, a lot like a crocodile. Its fin bones include the first hints of fingers.

name: Hyneria
fact: A giant river predator with fangs, big enough to eat the first four-legged animals that shared its streams.

name: Ichthyostega
c: Amphibians & early tetrapods › First four-legged animals
fact: One of the first four-legged animals. Its hind feet had seven toes — five-fingered hands came later. It probably hauled itself along like a seal rather than walking.

name: Jaekelopterus
fact: The largest arthropod ever known — a sea scorpion longer than a person. One claw alone is 46 cm long.

name: Gemuendina
fact: An armoured fish flattened like a ray, with wing-like fins — but no relation to rays at all.

name: Drepanaspis
fact: A jawless fish as flat as a frying pan, with its mouth on top of its head.
know: The Hunsrück Slate was mined for roofing tiles. X-rays of quarried slabs reveal fossils with legs, gills and tentacles invisible on the surface.

name: Holoptychius
fact: A lobe-finned river predator. At Dura Den, Scotland, a whole shoal died together when their pool dried out.

name: Gogonasus
fact: A reef fish whose fin bones and head show steps toward four-legged animals — including a large opening on top of its head for breathing air.

name: Ventastega
c: Amphibians & early tetrapods › First four-legged animals
fact: An animal halfway between fish and four-legged animal: a tetrapod skull with a fishy tail fin.

name: Zachełmie trackmaker
size: Up to about 2.5 m (from footprint size)
c: Amphibians & early tetrapods › First four-legged animals
fact: Footprints with toes, left on a tidal flat in Poland — 18 million years older than Tiktaalik. The animal itself has never been found.
debate: If they really are tetrapod tracks (2010), four-legged animals existed far earlier than their bones suggest. Some argue fishes could have made similar marks.

name: Attercopus
fact: A spider relative that could make silk but had no spinnerets to weave it — and a long tail. Silk came before webs.

name: Palaeocharinus
fact: A spider-like hunter (a trigonotarbid) from the Rhynie Chert, with book lungs so well preserved you can see the leaf-like breathing plates.

name: Rhynia
fact: A leafless stem plant turned to stone by silica-rich hot-spring water so quickly that individual cells survive.

name: Tutusius
c: Amphibians & early tetrapods › First four-legged animals
fact: One of the first four-legged animals found in Africa, named after Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Its home lay inside the Antarctic Circle of the time — so the move onto land was not just a tropical story.
know: It is known from a single shoulder bone, found in rock cut through for a road.
